name: Money Representation and Rounding
intent: Store money as whole numbers of the smallest currency unit plus a currency code, pick one written-down rounding rule and rounding point, and split or convert amounts so that not a single cent is lost or invented.
scenario: A checkout totals a cart of 6 lines (subtotal 178.08) with 10% tax. The cart service keeps prices as floating point dollars, and the payment provider keeps whole cents. The cart says 195.89, the provider says 195.90, and the two disagree by 1 cent. The same team then splits a 100.00 bill three ways and converts the cart to yen.
problem: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly: 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3, and 1.005 is stored as slightly less than 1.005. Tiny errors are harmless in a physics model and expensive in money, because an amount that lands exactly on a half cent rounds the wrong way, two systems that round differently disagree by a cent, and a reconciliation report fills up with differences nobody can explain. Splitting 100.00 three ways by dividing gives 99.99, so a cent vanishes, and converting between currencies adds a second rounding step on top.

howItWorks.title: Never use binary floating point for money
howItWorks.text: A float holds a binary fraction, and most decimal amounts (0.10, 1.005, 19.99) have no exact binary form, so every operation carries a tiny error. It shows up when an amount lands exactly on a rounding boundary: the tax on a line of 21.15 at 10% is exactly 2.115, but a double calculates 2.1149999999999998, so it rounds down to 2.11 instead of up to 2.12. Decimal types (Decimal, BigDecimal, decimal) are exact for decimal fractions and are fine for calculations. For storage and over the wire, whole numbers are simplest.

howItWorks.title: Whole numbers of the minor unit, plus a currency code
howItWorks.text: Store 1999 and USD, not 19.99. The minor unit is the smallest amount of the currency, and its exponent (the number of decimal places) depends on the currency: typically 2 for dollars and euros, 0 for the yen, 3 for the Kuwaiti dinar. The amount 1234 is 12.34 USD, 1234 JPY or 1.234 KWD, so an amount without a currency code is meaningless and the code is what tells you how to display and round it. ISO 4217 lists the codes and exponents. Integers add, subtract and compare exactly, and the database, the API and the ledger all agree on them.

howItWorks.title: Pick one rounding rule and one rounding point, and write them down
howItWorks.text: Rounding appears wherever a result has more precision than the unit: a percentage (tax, discount, fee), a division, a conversion. The rule decides ties: half up always rounds an exact half upwards, half even (banker's rounding) rounds it to the nearest even cent so ties do not push totals one way, truncating drops the fraction. The point decides where: tax rounded on each line and then added is not always the same as tax on the subtotal, rounded once. Either can be right, as long as the price, the invoice, the provider and the ledger all use the same one. Do the arithmetic in integers with the division last.

howItWorks.title: Split by allocation, not by division
howItWorks.text: Dividing 100.00 by 3 gives 33.33 three times, which adds up to 99.99. The largest remainder method fixes it: compute each share with integer division (33.33 each), count the cents left over (1), and give one extra cent to the shares with the largest remainders, usually the first ones when they tie. The parts are 33.34, 33.33 and 33.33 and they add up to exactly 100.00. The same method works for weights (a 5:3:2 split), for spreading a discount over lines, and for dividing a fee between parties.

howItWorks.title: Convert currencies with a precise rate and round once, at the end
howItWorks.text: A rate such as 149.2500 is a decimal number, so keep it as an integer (1492500 with 4 decimal places) or a decimal type, and say how many places it has. Convert in minor units, taking each currency's exponent into account, and round once, when you reach the final amount in the target currency. Rounding every line and adding gives a result that can differ from rounding the sum by several minor units. Store the original amount, the rate and the converted amount together, so the number can be explained later.

pros: Integer arithmetic is exact: sums, differences and comparisons never drift, in any language or database
One representation can be used in the database, the API, events and the ledger without translation
A written rounding rule and point makes every system produce the same cent, so reconciliation has nothing to explain
Allocation guarantees that the parts add up to the whole
cons: Every display and every input needs the currency's exponent, so the code needs a currency table instead of a blanket divide-by-100
Percentages, rates and conversions need careful integer scaling: the intermediate numbers get large
A rule such as half even surprises people who expect half up, so it has to be documented for finance and customers
Existing float data and APIs need a migration, and a unit mistake (cents versus dollars) is easy to make and silent
whenToUse: Anything that stores, adds, compares or transmits amounts of real money: prices, balances, invoices, fees, payouts
APIs and events between services, where the amount and currency should travel together as integers
Totals that must match another system exactly, such as a payment provider, a tax authority or a ledger
whenNotToUse: Estimates and analytics where a tiny error does not matter, such as a forecast, a chart or a model score
Amounts that need more precision than a cent by design (a fuel price per litre, a cloud price per million requests): keep a finer unit or a decimal type until the final charge
Values that are not money: a rating, a ratio or a duration does not need a currency code
pitfalls: Parsing a price such as "19.99" into a float on the way in and multiplying by 100 later: 19.99 * 100 is not exactly 1999 in a double
Assuming every currency has 2 decimals, so yen are charged 100 times too little or too much and dinars lose a digit
Rounding at every step of a calculation, so errors accumulate, instead of once at the end
Using a language's default round(): some round half to even, others half up, and a float tie is not a real tie
Dividing a bill or a fee and sending out the parts without checking that they add up to the whole
Storing an amount without its currency, or the converted amount without the rate and date that produced it

roles.label: Shopper
roles.description: Sees prices in a currency and expects the total to be the sum of what they see.

roles.label: Cart service
roles.description: Adds up the lines and calculates tax, then sends the total to payment.

roles.label: Rounding rule
roles.description: The written decision on how a fraction of a cent is rounded, and where.

roles.label: Payment provider
roles.description: Charges the amount it receives, in whole minor units of one currency.

roles.label: Ledger
roles.description: Stores the amounts as integers and must agree with every other system to the cent.

quiz.question: A service keeps prices as floating point dollars. Its daily revenue total is sometimes a cent away from the payment provider's report. What is the most robust fix?
options: Round to two decimals after each addition, so the error cannot grow.
Hold every amount as integer minor units with a currency code and do all arithmetic on those integers.
Switch to a 32-bit float so the errors are smaller and rarely reach a cent.
Add up the prices in a different order, so the small errors cancel out.
quiz.explanation: Floats cannot hold most decimal amounts exactly, so errors are built in, and rounding after each step does not remove them. Integer minor units are exact, and the currency code says what a unit means. A smaller float type makes the error larger, and summing in another order only moves the problem.

quiz.question: A restaurant bill of 100.00 is split between 3 people. The app charges each person 33.33. What is wrong, and what fixes it?
options: Nothing is wrong, because rounding each share to the nearest cent is the correct rule.
Each person should be charged 33.34, so that the restaurant is never underpaid.
A cent is missing: allocate the leftover cent to a share, giving 33.34, 33.33 and 33.33.
The app should keep 33.333 per person and round only when the card is charged.
quiz.explanation: Three shares of 33.33 add up to 99.99, so one cent is lost. Largest remainder allocation floors each share and hands out the leftover cents, so the parts always add up to the whole. Charging 33.34 each would invent 2 cents, and a card cannot be charged a fraction of a cent.

quiz.question: A payment API accepts an integer amount and a currency code. A client sends amount 5000 with currency JPY. How much is charged?
options: 5000 yen, because the yen has no minor unit and the integer is the yen amount.
50 yen, because every currency is divided by 100 to get the amount.
50.00 yen, because the amount is always in cents and is shown with 2 decimals.
5 yen, because the API takes thousandths for currencies without cents.
quiz.explanation: The exponent depends on the currency: typically 2 for dollars, 0 for yen and 3 for dinars. For JPY the minor unit is the yen itself, so 5000 means 5000 yen. Dividing everything by 100 charges yen customers a hundredth of the price.
